995.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
995.hook: a student begs to be saved, and the teacher answers: fear not, and then, nobody can eat your dinner for you
995.carry: there's no one to free you but yourself
995.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta the teacher, the guru, is held to be essential for showing the way, while the student is expected to reflect and meditate on the teaching personally until it becomes their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Vivekachudamani calls seeking your own nature bhakti. To love the truth of who you are.

The student arrives at the teacher's feet in a state. In the Vivekachudamani he describes himself as scorched, caught in the forest fire of the world, shaken by the winds of misfortune. He has no list of questions. He has one request: save me. It's a request people carry into doctors' offices and counselors' rooms too. What a teacher says first, in that moment, shapes everything after. The book records it. And a little later, it records something harder.
screen: `THE STUDENT ARRIVES SCORCHED.` → `ONE REQUEST: SAVE ME.` → `WHAT DOES THE TEACHER SAY?`

segments.voice: The guru's first words, in paraphrase: fear not, wise one. There is no danger for you. There is a way across this ocean, the way the sages crossed, and I will show it to you. That's comfort, plainly given. No lecture on why the student is suffering. Just: you're not lost; there's a road. Then the student finds his questions. What is bondage? How did it come? How does it stay? How do I get free? The teacher praises him for asking. Then comes the harder part. A father in debt, the text says, has sons and others to pay it off. But for bondage, there's no one to free you but yourself. Someone else can lift a heavy load from your head. Hunger, though, goes away only when you eat. A sick person gets well by taking the medicine and keeping to the diet, not by someone else doing it for them. Later the text sharpens it: an illness isn't cured by saying the word medicine without drinking it. Fear not, and nobody can do this for you. They sound opposite, but the book holds them together. In the book, the teacher really can show the way, and does. What he can't do is walk it in the student's place. On this path, jnana isn't handed over like a parcel. It has to be eaten, so to speak, by the one who is hungry. That isn't harsh. It's the respect you give a grown friend: I'll sit with you, and I trust you to stand up.
screen: `FEAR NOT. THERE IS A WAY ACROSS.` · `A DEBT CAN BE PAID BY OTHERS.` · `HUNGER ENDS ONLY WHEN YOU EAT.` · `SAYING MEDICINE DOESN'T CURE.` · then, large: `I'LL SHOW YOU. YOU WALK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been hoping someone else would fix for you, a worry, a habit, a decision, and hold it lightly while the teacher's words land: fear not, there is a way across. After a few breaths, ask without any scolding what one small step on it is yours alone to take, and just see it clearly. If you pray, you can hold both the comfort and the step together.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani a teacher can show it, but like food or medicine, it works only for the one who takes it.
Your line: there's no one to free you but yourself. The teacher shows the road; the student walks it. Day nine hundred ninety-five, done.

996.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
996.hook: a bee stays too long inside a lotus, and the petals close at dusk
996.carry: which sense has hold of you
996.howItsDone: Some students of the Vivekachudamani memorize short verses like this one and recall them during the day, using them to notice where the senses are pulling attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fear not, there's a way across, and nobody can eat your dinner for you. There's no one to free you but yourself.

A bee works its way deep into a lotus on a pond, late in the afternoon, drunk on the scent, and stays. And stays. The light goes gold, then gray. The petals begin to fold inward, slowly, the way lotuses close at evening, and the bee is still inside. The Vivekachudamani puts the bee in a short list of creatures, each one caught by a single sense. Then it turns to the reader and asks a question.
screen: `A BEE INSIDE A LOTUS.` → `THE PETALS CLOSE.` → `A LIST, AND A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. The deer, the elephant, the moth, the fish and the bee: these five die, each bound by one of the five senses, sound, touch, form, taste and smell. What then of a person, bound by all five? The old explanations fill in each picture. The deer is drawn by a hunter's music. The elephant by touch. The moth flies into the flame it can't stop looking at. The fish takes the bait for the taste. And the bee stays in the closing lotus for the smell. Each one is ruined by something good: music, touch, light, food, fragrance. None of them is evil. That's the sharp edge of the verse. It doesn't say the senses are wicked. It says a creature pulled along by even one of them can lose everything, and asks what happens to someone pulled by all five at once. You might expect a book about jnana to stay in the head. This verse brings it right down to the body: what you look at, what you reach for, where your attention gets towed. On this path, discernment, viveka, isn't only a thought about what lasts. It's noticing, in the moment, which sense has hold of you, and whether you chose it. The moth doesn't decide anything. It just flies. A person can notice the pull before the wings move. The text treats that small, practical noticing as part of the road to the larger kind of knowing.
screen: `DEER, ELEPHANT, MOTH, FISH, BEE.` · `EACH CAUGHT BY ONE SENSE.` · `WHAT OF ONE CAUGHT BY ALL FIVE?` · `NOTICE THE PULL BEFORE THE WINGS MOVE.` · then, large: `WHICH SENSE HAS HOLD OF YOU?`

segments.voice: Go through the senses one at a time, slowly, the way the verse lists them: the sound in the room, the weight of the body on the seat, the light behind your eyelids, what's on the tongue, the smell of the air. Then ask, quietly, which of these pulls at you most, and just see it, without pushing it away. If you pray, you can offer that sense back as your prayer.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani it starts small: seeing which sense has hold of you, before it carries you off.
Your line: which sense has hold of you. The moth just flies; a person can notice first. See you tomorrow.

997.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
997.hook: a coil lies across the garden path at dusk, and the Vivekachudamani asks what happens when someone brings a lamp
997.howItsDone: In Advaita teaching, the rope taken for a snake is an image used to explain adhyasa: the Self mistaken for the body and mind, set right by knowing rather than by effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the bee in the closing lotus: five creatures, each caught by a single sense. Which sense has hold of you?

A coil lies across the garden path at dusk. Someone walking home stops dead. It's long, it's curved, it might have moved. The heart pounds, the breath goes short, and they're already backing toward the gate. Then a neighbor steps out with a lamp. It's a rope, left lying there after somebody tied up the gate. Nothing on the path has changed. The rope was a rope the whole time. But the fear was real, and so was the step backward. The Vivekachudamani puts that small scene to work.
screen: `A COIL ON THE PATH AT DUSK.` → `A LAMP.` → `IT WAS ALWAYS A ROPE.`

segments.voice: When the teacher wants to show the student what has gone wrong, one picture he reaches for is the rope and the snake. In paraphrase: through not knowing, a rope is taken for a snake, and fear follows. Through not knowing, the Self is taken for the body, the mind, the restless one who worries, and suffering follows. The teaching's name for that mistake is adhyasa, superimposition: laying one thing on top of another. The snake is laid on the rope. The small, anxious I is laid on the Self. Now notice what the cure is not. Nobody kills the snake. Nobody runs for a stick, or better boots, or a long practice of being brave around snakes. That would be fighting something that isn't there. The cure is a lamp. Light falls on the rope, and the snake is simply gone, as long as the light stays on. That's jnana on this path: not collecting facts, but knowing that removes a mistake. And the rope never needed fixing. On this reading, the Self was never actually bound; the binding belonged to the seeing. That's why, two days ago, the teacher insisted the student look for themselves. A lamp held by someone else helps. But the snake only disappears for the one whose own eyes see the rope.
screen: `A ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `ADHYASA: ONE THING LAID ON ANOTHER.` · `NOBODY KILLS THE SNAKE.` · `THE CURE IS A LAMP.` · then, large: `THE ROPE NEVER NEEDED FIXING.`

segments.voice: Let the breath find its own pace. Before long a thought will arrive dressed as a fact about you: I'm tired, I'm behind, I'm not good at this. Don't argue with it or chase it off; hold a small lamp to it, and notice that it's a thought, appearing, and what is aware of it appearing. It may stay or go; either way, keep the light on.
Jnana. Knowing, on the path of knowing: not a pile of facts, but the seeing that turns the snake back into a rope.
Your line: a rope in poor light. The snake was never there to fight. Good to see you today.

998.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
998.hook: an arrow is already flying when the archer sees the tiger was a cow
998.carry: not mistaking the weather for yourself
998.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers often explain the jivanmukta, the one free while living, through prarabdha karma: actions already begun play out in the body's life, while knowledge ends the mistaken sense of being bound by them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana as a lamp: a rope taken for a snake, and a fear that ends without a fight. Today, the last day in the Vivekachudamani.

An archer at the edge of a field sees a striped shape in the long grass. A tiger. He lets the arrow go, and in the half second after it leaves the string, the shape lifts its head. It's a cow. He knows the truth now, completely. But the arrow is already in the air, and knowing can't call it back. The Vivekachudamani tells this little story late in the book to answer a hard question. If knowing sets someone free, why does the free person still have a body, still get hungry, still catch a cold?
screen: `A STRIPED SHAPE IN THE GRASS.` → `THE ARROW IS ALREADY FLYING.` → `WHY DOES THE FREE ONE STILL CATCH COLDS?`

segments.voice: Its answer, in paraphrase: actions set in motion before knowing dawns are like that arrow. Their name is prarabdha, the karma that has already begun. Knowing doesn't stop them; they play out, and the body that came with them lives on until they're spent. What knowing stops is the next arrow. The one who sees clearly no longer draws the bow from fear, from grabbing, from the old mistake about who they are. The book calls such a person jivanmukta, free while living. Not a ghost or a statue: someone who eats, sleeps and walks to the market like everyone else. The difference is inside. The text compares it to waking from a dream. In the dream there was a palace, a debt, a chase down a hallway. Nobody wakes up and pays the dream's debts. That's how the free one holds the body's life, the book says: lightly, as something seen, not something that defines them. Then a qualifier: prarabdha holds only while someone takes themselves to be the body. For the one who knows, it says, even that falls away. So the selections come into one view. A student desperate to be free. A teacher showing the binding was a mistake, a rope taken for a snake. The cure, jnana. And the one who knows still lives an ordinary life, old arrows landing one by one, no new ones drawn. Some readers find that ending a relief. On this account, freedom isn't a life with no weather in it. It means not mistaking the weather for yourself.
screen: `PRARABDHA: THE ARROW ALREADY FLYING.` · `KNOWING STOPS THE NEXT ARROW.` · `JIVANMUKTA: FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `LIKE WAKING FROM A DREAM.` · then, large: `NO NEW ARROWS DRAWN.`

segments.voice: Notice whatever the body is carrying right now, an ache, tiredness, a full stomach, a restless foot, and treat each one as an arrow already in flight: it will land, so let it. Then watch the mind for the next arrow, the reaction that wants to be drawn, a complaint, a plan, a worry. Notice it, and leave the bow where it is.
Jnana. Knowing that frees: it can't call back the arrows already flying, but it stops drawing new ones.
Your line: not mistaking the weather for yourself. The old arrows land, and no new ones are drawn. That's day nine hundred ninety-eight.

999.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
999.hook: a king asks three questions in one breath, and a sage answers without offering him a single thing to do
999.carry: happy, at peace and free, right now
999.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita is read and studied by students of Advaita Vedanta, often slowly with a teacher, and some recite or chant its Sanskrit verses; it is a dialogue in which King Janaka asks and the sage Ashtavakra answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vivekachudamani ended with an arrow already flying and a person free while living: not mistaking the weather for yourself. Today, a new book on the same path.

Before the book, there's a boy, and the Mahabharata tells his story. Still in his mother's womb, it says, he heard his father reciting the sacred texts and spoke up to correct him. The father, stung, cursed the child, and he was born bent in eight places. So he was called Ashtavakra, eight bends. Later, still young, he walked into the court of King Janaka of Videha and out-argued the court's champion in debate. The book named for him, the Ashtavakra Gita, puts the sage and the king in a quieter room, alone. And the king opens with a question.
screen: `A BOY WHO CORRECTED HIS FATHER.` → `BORN BENT IN EIGHT PLACES.` → `A SAGE AND A KING, ALONE.`

segments.voice: Janaka's first words, in paraphrase, are three questions in one breath. How is knowledge gained? How does freedom come? How is detachment reached? It's a busy man asking for a method. Ashtavakra's first answer sounds like ethics. If you want freedom, my child, leave the objects of the senses as you'd leave poison, and drink forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth like nectar. Then he turns sharply. You aren't earth, or water, or fire, or air, or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these, consciousness itself. A verse later comes the turn that gives the book its edge. If you set the body aside and simply rest in awareness, you are happy, at peace and free of bondage, right now. Not after the practices. Not at the end of the road. Now. That's how the Ashtavakra Gita reads. It hardly gives instructions; it keeps pointing at what the king already is. Over six days i'll walk through it in large steps: the king's question, a line about bondage and freedom, the king's awakening, the sage's test, a chapter about forgetting everything, and the last chapter's long litany. Some readers find it too abrupt to use. Others find the abruptness is the whole gift. It doesn't ask Janaka to become something new, only to stop overlooking what's already here.

segments.voice: Notice the body, its weight and warmth, then the sounds in the room and the thoughts drifting through. Then, gently, notice the noticing itself, the awareness in which all of them show up. Nothing to push away; just rest there, as the one who sees.

1000.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1000.hook: one verse says the one who takes themselves to be free is free, and the one who takes themselves to be bound is bound
1000.carry: the binding lives in the taking
1000.howItsDone: Students of the Ashtavakra Gita often memorize or recite individual verses in Sanskrit, and the verse on being free or bound is one that teachers quote when discussing how bondage, on this view, lies in identification rather than in the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita began: three questions from King Janaka, and a sage who said rest as the witness: happy, at peace and free, right now.

Free, if you take yourself as free. Bound, if you take yourself as bound. That's the line, in paraphrase, from the first chapter of the Ashtavakra Gita. And the sage doesn't call it his own discovery. He says it's a saying people repeat, and the saying is true: as the mind holds itself, so it goes. A strange thing to hear on the thousandth day of anything. A thousand days could feel like finally getting somewhere, or like miles still to go. This verse quietly asks about both: who is doing the counting?
screen: `FREE, IF YOU TAKE YOURSELF AS FREE.` → `A SAYING, AND IT'S TRUE.` → `WHO IS DOING THE COUNTING?`

segments.voice: Read quickly, the verse sounds like a poster on a gym wall: believe in yourself and anything is possible. The verses around it show it means something stranger. A few verses earlier, the sage tells Janaka that bondage is this one thing: seeing someone else as the seer, rather than yourself. He says the king has been bitten by the black snake of egoism, the thought, I am the doer. Drink the nectar of faith in the thought, I am not the doer, he says, and be happy. Then comes the line: one who holds that they're free is free; one who holds that they're bound is bound. So it isn't positive thinking, think hard enough and life gets better. It says the binding was never in the world. It was in the taking, in what consciousness took itself to be. Ashtavakra's word for free is mukta. On his account, nobody builds their way to mukta. They stop insisting they're bound. A thousand days in, that cuts both ways, and the text wouldn't mind. The days of practice are real: the sitting, the reading, the lamps and the songs. But this book would say the one who sat for all of them was never in a cell. Freedom, on its account, isn't a reward at the end of a long climb. It's a fact about the climber, there on day one, and on day one thousand.

segments.voice: Aho. It's a Sanskrit cry of wonder, the sound someone makes when a thing turns out bigger than expected. It's how King Janaka opens the second chapter. In the first, he asked his three questions and listened. Now the teacher falls silent and the student speaks, and he doesn't ask anything. He exclaims. A few verses in, he does something that makes a first-time reader look twice. He bows to himself.
screen: `AHO: A CRY OF WONDER.` → `THE STUDENT STOPS ASKING.` → `THE KING BOWS TO HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Chapter two begins, in paraphrase: Aho, I am spotless, at peace, pure awareness, beyond nature. All this time I've been fooled by delusion. Then Janaka reaches for the sea. As waves and foam and bubbles are nothing other than water, so this whole world, flowing out of the Self, is nothing other than the Self. A wave can rise high or crash on the rocks; it never stops being water. Then the verses that make people sit up. Wonderful am I, Janaka says. Salutation to me. Namo mahyam. I remain, even when the whole world, from the creator down to a blade of grass, is destroyed. On the surface that sounds like a king who's had too much praise. But the I in these verses isn't Janaka with a crown and a treasury. It's the awareness he was pointed to on the first day, the witness. Bowing to that, he bows to what he takes to be in everything, the blade of grass included. The line is fine, and the text walks it. On this reading, the small I that wants credit is exactly what has dropped away. What's left can't be flattered; there's no one left to flatter. That's why the chapter sounds like joy, not vanity. A man who thought he was a wave has just found out he's water. And he doesn't explain it. He sings.
screen: `SPOTLESS, AT PEACE, PURE AWARENESS.` · `WAVES, FOAM AND BUBBLES ARE WATER.` · `NAMO MAHYAM: SALUTATION TO ME.` · `NOT THE KING. THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `THE WAVE FINDS IT'S WATER.`

segments.voice: Watch thoughts and feelings rise and fall like waves: a plan, a memory, a flicker of worry. Don't calm them; just watch each one rise and sink back, and notice what they rise in, the awareness itself, the water under the waves. If a wave seems big, let it be big; it's still water.
